heading: JSON in every language
body: In every Yon language, Yon turns an ordinary return value that is compatible with JSON into JSON text. It does this once, with status 200 and application/json. You do not build a response object. To encode and decode JSON yourself, use the JSON APIs of the language. Java and Kotlin give Json.parse and Json.stringify. Rust gives Json::parse and Json::stringify, which can fail. C# can use System.Text.Json directly. Dart can use dart:convert. Go can use encoding/json. Tachyon reads the fields of Go types in `server/models/` only. A Go type from another package, such as `json.RawMessage`, `http.Header`, `time.Time` or `spec.Document` from your native packages in `server/packages/`, is an open JSON value in a model field, a route parameter or a route result: Go's `encoding/json` reads and writes it, and Tachyon accepts any JSON there. A field tagged `json:"-"` is not part of the JSON at all. A `*http.Request`, a `context.Context` or a multipart file is not JSON data, so a model field of that type fails with `TY2015`: read it from the `*http.Request` parameter of the route method instead, like an `HttpServletRequest` or `MultipartFile` parameter in Spring. A returned model is written with the names of its fields. C# writes its PascalCase properties in camelCase, so `Name` becomes `name`, in normal answers and in streams. A model that extends another model keeps the fields of its parent, such as a Java class that extends a model or a Dart model that passes `super.name` to its parent. JSON that is not valid is rejected. A returned string stays a JSON string, even if its contents look like JSON. To send a custom status, headers, cookies or a raw body, answer with the language's own response, such as a Fetch Response, an http::Response or a Go `*http.Response` with `Set-Cookie` in its `Header`; this is the role of Spring's `ResponseEntity`.
